Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM:	Reports
are printed in the newspapers as to the recruiting not being satisfactory. I have been assured privately that the recruiting is satisfactory to the Government. Does the Government care to make a statement to the House and to the country as to whether the recruiting at present is satisfactory to them?
Major-General HUGHES (Minister of Militia): So far as my department is concerned, and that is the one chiefly interested, I shall reply to the hon. gentleman's question by giving a number of instances. A few weeks ago, in six hours, 650 men were raised for a cavalry regiment. In some towns in Eastern Ontario, within 24 hours after the call of the third contingent, we had far more men than the quota desired. In places where the men have not responded it has been due to the fact that the corps have not been encouraged, or that we have not had accommodation wherein to place the men just at the time. We have now every regiment in Canada up to full strength. Edmonton recruited in twelve days up to full strength. The Nova Scotia cavalry regiment is over strength to-day.	I could
raise a regiment in Cape Breton in four hours if I wanted to. I am now speaking from returns that I have received. In short, at the present moment, according to the returns we have got, I could raise three more contingents inside of three weeks, if necessary.

On the Orders of the Day being called:
Major-General HUGHES:	In answer to
some questions asked by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) a day or so ago regarding the " discarding in great quantities at Salisbury Plains of wagons, harness, Ross rifles, etc.," inquiry reveals that the wagons and harness have been subjected to four months of extremely hard usage, very bad weather, hauling very heavy loads over very rough roads and through deep mud. Naturally, the wear and tear was great. New wagons from Canada were not available, therefore it was deemed wise and proper to outfit the Canadians on going into the field in this great struggle with the best wagons on hand. Accordingly, they were	supplied with the
new wagons from the British stores. Regarding the harness the same holds good. The harness had been in use all winter and it was not deemed advisable to send the boys to the front with the old harness so they wrere equipped when leaving for France with the best harness available at the time. There may be doubt
whether the receipt of his pay as an officer in the expeditionary force would disqualify him from being elected, blit when this Bill is passed there can be no question based on the fact that he receives such pay, and I do not know of any other ground on which he could be disqualified. In the Election Act as it now stands, I think there are provisions whereby a man absent from the country may be nominated without his express consent being obtained. I do not remember the exact provisions, but I am satisfied that that is covered by the present Act. It might be that under the Act sought to be amended by this Bill, a man with the expeditionary forces would be ineligible for election by the fact of his receiving pay, but this Bill will remedy that. In the law as it now stands there is a provision to exempt miliua officers, but the men with the expeditionary forces are not serving in the capacity of officers of the militia of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned last night, I was dealing with some criticisms of the Government made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). A few minutes before the adjournment I was dealing with the charge that he had made that the Government had advanced large sums of money, many millions of dollars, to Mackenzie and Mann. I think the hon. gentleman could not help but know that this Government have advanced no money to Mackenzie and Mann, nor have they advanced money to either Mackenzie or Mann. It is true they made a loan to the Canadian Northern railway system, a loan amply secured by mortgages intended to pay off certain liabilities and complete the work of that transcontinental railway. But the charge is made that the company will be unable to complete their work and that the whole railway system will 'be thrown on the hands of the Government. If it is, if the worst comes to the worst, and that should unfortunately happen, the Gove n-ment has amply secured the people of this country by seeing that the amount of money they have loaned shall go into the paying off of the liabilities of the railway as a system and for the completion of the road so that if they ever have to take it over as an entity it will represent not only the value of the road when they made the loan but the added value after the expenditure of that money upon it. Mackenzie and Mann did not benefit personally or as a corporation by the amount of money advanced by this Government. Under the peculiar circumstances that have arisen it was absolutely impossible for the Government to allow this work to go by default. It was near completion, it served a large stretch of country; to have allowed it to go by default would have damaged our interests in the monetary markets of the world, and there was no other course open to the Government than to 'See that the work was completed. I want to say again, that the Canadian Northern matter and the Grand Trunk Pacific matter were twins that were left destitute upon the Conservative doorstep and the Conservative party had to take charge of them, although they deny parentage.
I want now to deal with a few of the 
points raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). He seems to have a vast fund of sympathy for the western farmer. I am a farmer myself, but not one of those farmers who derive their information in regard to farming conditions in some lawyer's office or in some doctor's studio or in the sanctum of some printing office. I derive my knowledge of farming conditions out on the farm itself, where I go and throw off my coat and get to work just the same as the other men upon the farm.
Let me look at the representation from the West. I look at the representative for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), and I see the ex-Minister of the Interior, who derives his information with regard to farming conditions in the sanctum of his printing office. Then I go down to Medicine Hat and I- find that the representative for that constituency (Mr. Buchanan) also gets his knowledge of farming operations in his printing office. I now come to Moosejaw and I see that horny-handed son of the soil, the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles), whose knowledge of farming conditions enables him to conduct his business successfully as a lawyer. He issues writs against the farmers, occasionally charging them $5 per case for making out the papers. Then we have the genial member for Eegina (Mr. Martin), another farmer from the West, who also derives his information with regard to farming matters and his sympathy for the farmers in his lawyer's office. I go south a little to Assiniboia, and I see the hon. member for that constituency (Mr. Turriff), another robust farmer-ex-civil servant and retired wealthy gentleman. I come next to Qu'Appelle and there we have a gentleman (Mr. Thomson) who also occupies a lawyer's office; but I believe he has a farm and he has probably a little knowledge of actual farming conditions. I now go across to Humboldt, the hon. member for which (Mr. Neely) derives his knowledge and inspirations in regard to farming conditions in the West by feeling the pulses of his patients and looking at their tongues occasionally, and charging them so much in each case. I next go to Saskatoon where we have another farmer (Mr. McCraney) entering suits and collecting bills in the interest of the farmers of that section-another lawyer. It is quite right to have a proper criticism of the Government, to have many farmers sitting in Opposition and keeping the Government straight and bringing the case of the farmer to its attention from time to

time; but seriously, some time I would like to see some seat on the Opposition side occupied by a real farmer, one of those men who are actually suffering from the conditions that prevail in the West at the present time.
It will be conceded by those familiar with farming conditions in the West that the farmer has not everything that he would wish; that he has difficulties in his way. He has not those large centres of population that have been created in the East by large manufactories and institutions of that nature, and practically all the product of his toil must find a market a long distance away from the source of production. That is a handicap which ought to be taken into consideration by any Government. It is the duty of the Government to do everything possible to help out the western farmer. There are matters of transportation, assistance to railways, the making free or the cheapening as far as possible of these articles that must be purchased by the western as well as by the eastern farmer, but especially by the western farmer. There is also the providing of elevator facilities where they are lacking and for a proper inspection of the grain, and the ensuring that the farmer gets a just return for his produce and proper grading. These are matters that have engaged the attention of the present Government since it came into power, and it has done a great deal towards assisting the western farmer.
The principal product of the western soil, as we all know, is wheals and from time to time hon gentlemen opposite, since they have occupied the seats of the Opposition, have bewailed the position of the farmers in the West with regard to their great standard cereal. They say that we ought to have opened the markets of the United States; that we 'ought to have accepted the offer they made, Toy the acceptance of which they say we would have provided a wonderful market for the western farmer. I have given this matter a great deal of attention. For two years I have watched the markets of the United States and the markets of Canada as far as they have been reported in the press and during those two years there have not been more than two or three days on which the market price of wheat at Winnipeg has not been greater than the market price for the same grade of wheat at Minneapolis. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and other hon. gentlemen
who usually follow his lead with regard to this matter, have from time to time stated in this House that the price received by the western farmer for his wheat has been reduced by the amount of duty charged on it when it goes into the United States, and they have figured out tables to show the tremendous loss sustained by the western farmers in that way. Therefore, when the proposition was made in the fall of 1913 by the American Government to reduce the duty upon wheat, a proposition which finally carried reducing the duty by fifteen cents per bushel, naturally the western farmer, if he believed the teaching of the hon. member for Edmonton, would expect that the price of his wheat would be increased by fifteen cents per bushel. As a farmer in the West and at that time having wheat in my granary and being busily engaged in teaming it to the elevator in town, and believing that this reduction would not make a cent of difference in the price of the wheat that the farmers of the West had to sell, I went right on disposing of my wheat, knowing that in one or two or three weeks the Bill before the United States Congress would pass and become law.
I expected no advantage from the reduction in the duty. In course of time the Bill providing for that reduction was put on the statute book of the United States. I still had wheat to sell, and I went on selling it. And I am here to say that the farmers of the West do not benefit by the fraction of a cent by that reauction of fifteen cents in the duty on wheat.
As I have said, the price of wheat in Minneapolis has been almost steadily lower than the price in Winnipeg. I speak especially of No. I Northern which is the grade that is quoted in tne press daily. Let me read the report as given in the Citizen of this morning, showing the market conditions in Minneapolis and Winnipeg. In Winnipeg, No. 1 Northern is quoted- at I1.53J; in Minneapolis, No. 1 Northern is quoted at from $1.47J to $ 1.511, an average of $1.49, or a fraction over four cents higher in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis.
But my hon. friend may meet me with the statement that the grading under the State Grading Act in Minnesota is lower than on our side. True, the standard is not so highi But let me point out that the cash price of wheat as quoted in Minneapolis has very little to do with the State grade. In only four of the States of the American Union have they a State Grain Inspection Act, and even in those States

tne inspection is not compulsory. Let us suppose that a farmer in the West, finding all obstacles* removed to his shipping grain to Minneapolis, sends down a car and follows it to put it on the market. It is graded No. 1 Northern under the State Grain Inspection Act. He goes to a dealer, tells him what he has to sell and asks for an offer. The dealer says he cannot make a bid as he has not seen the wheat. " But," says the owner, " you do not need to see it; it is No. 1 Northern."	But the dealer
insists that he must see it; and the owner finds that he cannot get a bid until the would-be purchaser has seen the wheat. A great deal of the wheat sent to Minneapolis is sold to the millers, for they have there the largest milling concerns perhaps in the world, and certainly the largest on the American continent. So, our friend the western farmer, goes down to the miller who is buying many carloads of wheat daily. The miller says, " I never buy wheat on state grades; I will send my man up and look over your wheat and will make you an offer for it." The man goes up and looks over our friend's car and over the cars offered by his neighbours. He may buy them all; and there may be a difference of as much as five cents a bushel in the price offered for the several cars, though all are graded No. 1 Northern. So, there is very little reliance to be 4 p.m. placed on the figures given as to the cash prices of wheat in Minneapolis. But in any event, grade for grade, quality for quality, the price in Winnipeg for the last two years during which I have been looking into the matter has been better than the price in Minneapolis. To my personal knowledge wheat has been taken across the line and sold to Canadian elevators within that time. I have no doubt that under certain conditions and at certain times wheat may be teamed across from Canada to the other side and sold. A great deal of the wheat as disposed of in Minneapolis is sold on its quality and not on its grade under the State Grain Inspection Act. Over the rest of the United States they have all kinds of inspection-complete lack of uniformity. There has been an effort in the United States Congress for the last twenty-five years to get the Government of the United States to adopt a law enforceable throughout the Union. Those who favour that measure point out that there has been a great deal of complaint in England, Germany, France, the Netherlands and other wheat-buying countries in Europe about the lack of uniform grading in the United. 
States. In the case of grain from the United States, the grade is not enforceable, and if the wheat does not come up to grade the buyer has no redess. On at least two occasions, as pointed out by Senator McCumber on the introduction of his Bill last year, the grainimporting countries of Europe have met and, after athorough discussion of this matter, have passed resolutions appealing to the Government of the United States to have a law enacted that shall apply to that whole country. And Senator McCumber in his various addresses touching this matter when it was up for discussion last year, dealt exhaustively with the subject, and pointed out numberless resolutions passed by farmers' institutes and associations and by boards of trade in many localities, urging the United States to follow the example of Canada and have a uniform grade that would apply to the whole country. And it has been declared in many of the petitions sent in that the condition of the farmer in the Canadian west is vastly superior to that of the farmer of the western states in regard to the disposal of his wheat. Whether they are right in that or not I am not in a position to say. But I should think, taking the country over, there would be little difference in the condition of the western farmers on either side of the line. Both have the same disabilities arising out of the long haul to the seaboard. This great vexed question of transportation affects them as it affects us. The charges by the elevator men, by the insurance companies, by the transportation companies for ocean freights-all these things stand in their way as they stand in the way of the farmer of our West.
So that the adoption of any policy that would allow the free exchange of wheat between the two countries would fail to provide any remedy for the farmers of Western Canada. I am quite satisfied in regard to that matter. And the farmer in the Canadian west would lose the advantage he has to-day in the guarantees that go with his wheat by reason of the official inspection at Winnipeg as it passes through on its way to the ocean.
If American wheat could come across to Winnipeg, becomh merged with our wheat and find its way further east, our wheat would lose its individuality; it would practically become American wheat, and we would lose all the advantages that we now derive from our present system of grain inspection.
Permit me to call attention to another consideration that would militate against

the farmer of the West. When a good farmer happens to need money, he hurries his grain into the cars when the new crop comes in, in order that he may be among the first shippers, for if he succeeds in getting his wheat out early, he will get a better price than he would receive later. I am not now - ref erring to present conditions, which have been so *seriously affected by the war during the last few months; I am speaking of conditions as they have prevailed in the West, and as they will again prevail when the war is over. If we remove all obstacles to free interchange of wheat, and the people of the Western States put their grain upon the market a week, two weeks *or three weeks earlier than our farmers do, they will at once swamp the Winnipeg market with their wheat and our farmers will lose the advantage which they have enjoyed in past years in that respec', But we are told that there will be a large demand for our wheat; that we grow bet' ter wheat than they grow in the United States; that our friends to the south want Canadian wheat to grind with their softer wheat and are willing to pay a large price for it. In that way, our friends say, the farmers of the West will benefit to a large extent. I want to point out that our American friends have a much larger surplus of wheat than we have in Canada and, just as we have to find a market for our surplus wheat, they have to find a market for theirs. Any wheat, therefore, going into American channels from Canada would increase that surplus, and that surplus must find its way to some foreign country. I have not the shadow of a doubt,' viewing the whole situation generally, that under a system of free exchange we would purchase just as much American wheat as the people of the United States would purchase from us.
But, our friends say, freight conditions would be better. Let us look at that phase of the question for a moment. They say that there would be additional competition, and that the American railways, bidding for the carrying trade of the West, would reduce the price the farmers now have to pay in order to get their wheat to the head of the lakes or to the seaboard. I have given a little attention to the subject of freight rates in the Western States and to the seaboard, and I find, according to the commission which governs freight rates in the United States, that the rates are much the same as those prevailing in
Canada. I would remind hon. gentlemen also that if any farmer in the West wishes to send his wheat through American channels to the seaboard and across the ocean, there is absolutely nothing to prevent his doing so, and he has been doing so for years. Nothing hinders his using any railway in the United States for the shipment of his wheat. There is practically no duty on grain going through the United States to other countries. As I have said, the United States has a much larger surplus of wheat than we have; that surplus must find its way across the ocean-and they might just as well export Canadian wheat as any other kind of wheat. Another reason why they wish to handle Canadian wheat is in order to keep their vessels busy. If the Canadian shipper can get a reduction in rates of one-sixteenth of a cent by sending his wheat through the United States, naturally he will take advantage of the reduction by routing his wheat southwards. There is nothing in the statute books either of this country or of the United States to prevent our wheat going through United States channels.
The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) said that during the last two years there lias been no increase in the acreage sown in the great western country. I have an intimate knowledge of conditions prevailing in the West, as I have travelled over it a good deal, and I take issue with the hon. member in that regard. Any one who is conversant with conditions prevailing in the West knows that when a farmer breaks the prairie he has to keep it under cultivation; otherwise it will lapse back into a condition worse than its original state, and he will be the loser to the extent of a very large amount of money. The farmer is forced, therefore, to keep under cultivation such areas as have been broken and cultivated. 1 know by personal investigation that large areas have been brought, under cultivation in the last few years. I believe that the acreage in 1914 was considerably larger than that of 1913, and that the acreage in 1913 was greater than that of 1912; the same is true, I think, of every year since the great western country was first opened up. It is true that the amount of wheat grown in the West last year was less than that grown in previous years, but a great drouth had prevailed, with the result that the farmers suffered severely. In many sections of the western country the farmers had only a short crop, and in some portions of it they had no crop at all. This accounts for the fact that on the last

day of December, 1914, the amount of wheat shipped through Winnipeg was not half as large as it was on the same day of the previous year. The conditions for getting wheat out were infinitely better in 1914 than they were in 1913, inasmuch as threshing commenced much earlier, and the weather was favourable for cutting and threshing and for getting the grain to market.
Some people in the East, in discussing the subject of farming conditions in the West, are disposed to belittle the difficulties of the western farmer. They say that he does not deserve any special consideration; that he gets his land for nothing; that it is all ready to be worked, and that he is doing [DOT]better than the farmer of any other section of the country. My experience in the West, however, is that the western farmer has a pretty hard row to hoe. As a rule he goes out there as a poor man, without any money. He takes up his homestead, and in order to provide an equipment to work that 160 acies he is at the expense of approximately $2,000. Having no money he has to work for his neighbours. He finally succeeds in getting a little breakng done, he gets up a little shanty and works along as best he can under exceedingly great difficulties, because before he can plough a furrow or buy an outfit of his own, he must have at least four horses which would cost approximately $1,000. He has to have the harness and other attachments, he must have a plough, a spread harrow, a disc harrow, a seeder, and if he takes off his crop he must have a binder. He may succeed in purchasing some of these things on credit and finally, at the end of three years, he may be enabled to take out his patent. Usually he then rushes off to some mortgage company and borrows a large sum of money to pay off some of his debts and perhaps secure a few more implements; and this mortgage is for many years a heavy burden on him. That is a condition of affairs which no legislation that can be passed by either party in this House can remedy. That is a natural condition with men going into a country like that without capital, and our first duty should be to make it as easy as possible for them to secure some capital with which to go on. I think the Government of the country might well direct their energies in that direction. If they could find a solution of that difficulty they would do a great deal more for the farmer of the West than by finding markets for him that are already full, because finding a market for him across the border would be like find-
ing a market with his next neighbour who has 20,000 bushels of wheat himself and says: I do not need your wheat, I have wheat of my own and I will only buy your wheat in order that I may sell it again at an advance. That will be exactly the condition if our farmers try to find a market in the United States. I believe the Government have done something towards providing elevators in the West. I think they, might well work along in that direction in order that the farmer may be able to get his grain graded and raise money on it without having to dispose of it in a great hurry immediately after harvest, because it must be evident that every farmer there who has had to run nearly twelve months without money, finds that he must dispose of his grain as quickly as he cp.n; his creditors are crowding him, he has to pay off his bills for machinery, he has to give something to the blacksmith, the grocer, the harness-maker and many others, and he simply must have the cash. As time goes on and men get into better circumstances in the West, they are able to hold their grain. That would adequately describe the position of a number of people in the West to-day, perhaps more particularly in Manitoba and the older settled sections of Saskatchewan; but there are large areas dn Saskatchewan and Alberta where there are still many poor homesteaders struggling very hard to get a foothold in the country. There are many other ways in which we might be able to assist the settler in the West. My sympathies naturally go out to him because I have been there and I know something of his difficulties. When I am there, actually living out on the farm side by side with these men, going into their shanties, talking with them, working with them, exchanging work with them, attending their threshings and having them attend mine, knowing all about what they are doing, I feel that they deserve the very greatest consideration that can possibly be given them by the Government of this country. I do not know whether anything could be done in the way of rearranging our banking system so as to assist these people to get money when they need it, but I say this matter should be considered and I have no doubt it will receive consideration at the hands of the Government.
Referring to the charge that has been made that the Government has been letting the trade of this country go to the bow wows, I believe the Toronto Globe,-or some neighbour of the Globe politically, has made the charge that the whole trade policy of the

Government has gone to smash. That is the irresponsible utterance of the irresponsible editor of an irresponsible newspaper. Hon. gentlemen opposite have always been disposed in the past to measure up the prosperity of the country by the total of its exports and imports, and I want, just for a moment, to make a little comparison with regard to that matter. In 1910 we had imports coming into this country of $241,961,556, of dutiable goods; and of free goods, $143,873,547 or a total, dutiable and free, of $385,835,103. In 1914 we had an importation of dutiable goods of $425,324,576 and of free goods of $210,186,916, a total dutiable and free, of $635,511,492 or an increase of $249,676,389. The same would be measurably true with regard to our exports. I find that they also have increased by a very large amount. The total exports in 1910 were $279,247,551. In 1914 they were $431,588,439, or a balance in favour of the present Government of $152,340,888. I do not believe that the total amount of our exports and the total amount of our imports is an infallible barometer giving an unfailing index of the prosperity of a country, but that is the favourite argument of the hon. gentlemen opposite, and if there is anything in it the comparison is certainly largely in favour of the Government now occupying the Treasury Benches. Personally I think we might very largely decrease both our imports and exports, and yet be just as well off as we are to-day.
A great deal better off.

ture has declined, and declined enormously in Great Britain. They find that they cannot exist under the free trade conditions of that country. The farmer in Great Britain has all the advantages of great manufacturing centres right at his door. He can hitch up his team on the farm and find a market for everything he produces in the nearest market town, which will not be more than two or three miles away. If he wishes to buy, he can buy at his very door, where the goods are manufactured. He caii buy and sell at first hand. There are no transportation charges in either case. If farming can be benefited by free trade, surely under those conditions the farmers of Great Britain would be the wealthiest people in the face of the earth. But we find the agricultural industry there has declined and declined enormously. Would not free trade have an immeasurably worse effect in this country? I think it would.
Let us suppose we adopted the principle laid down by some hon. gentlemen opposite and did away with our customs duties in large measure, or altogether. That would have the effect of shutting up our factories and of throwing, a large number of men out of work. These men would naturally have to crowd out to the farms, or go to some other country. If they crowded out into the rural sections and became farmers, the production of the farms would largely increase; hut there would be a much less number of people to consume those products, and a vastly larger percentage of those products would have to find its way across the ocean to a foreign market, under all the disabilities I outlined a moment ago. The result would inevitably be that they would have to take less money for their products, and what advantage would that be? Then for manufactured articles, as there would be no competition in Canada, they would have to pay to foreign countries whatever they asked. They would certainly j>ay a larger sum than they pay today. I ask myself would the agriculturist be better off under such conditions? I say no, most emphatically no. For these reasons I feel that a reasonable measure of protection is absolutely indispensable to this country in its present condition. I believe we should have a protective tariff, not a tariff as high as Haman's gallows, but one giving a reasonable measure of protection. We in Canada to-day under our tariff policy recognize to some extent, the principle of free trade; we recognize the principle of tariff for revenue, and the prin-

ciple of protection. That is as true of the parties who occupied the treasury benches in years gone by as it is of the parties that occupies them to-day. Perhaps the only difference between us is as to the importance we attach to each of these various phases of policy. I think that tariff matters ought to be taken out of the political arena.	.
I believe there should be no party feeling in regard to it. We ought to have a tariff board which would deal with this matter independently of those who may be occupying the treasury benches. When such a proposition was laid before this House, discussed and carried in this House, the popular chamber which voices public opinion in this Dominion, the Bill was thrown out by the irresponsible body on the other side of this building.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would remind the hon. gentleman that such a remark is not permissible when referring to the other branch of this Parliament.

It has been said by way of criticism by hon. gentlemen opposite that such a tariff board might under certain circumstances show favouritism. The tariff board should be outside of political control or at least should be devoid of party politics. The Government of the country, or Parliament, should be allowed to name one member of that board and the Opposition might be allowed to name a member to see that no injustice was done to any manufacturer who might have his affairs investigated by the board. A representative of the great agricultural interests should be placed upon that bo'ard; the great manufacturing and mercantile interests might very well claim a representative upon that board, and the mining, lumbering and fishing industries might also very properly be represented upon it. The very best men in Canada, such as we have on the railway board, should find a place upon the board which should have authority to look into all complaints that might be laid before it, such as overcharging the public, or in one way or another taking advantage of the people. Such a board as that would he essential to the proper investigation of all such charges, and I do not know any good reason why the leaders on the Government side and the leaders on the Opposition side could not get together and agree upon such a board. I do not believe that the power should be placed in the hands of any board

to go right into a man's office, take his books and make known all his private affairs to his competitors and to the world generally. All investigations of that nature should be private, and a man's business should not be disclosed, but I would have the board of such a nature that there would be absolute confidence that fair play would be done. It would be a deterrent upon individuals here and there who might take * advantage of certain conditions to overcharge the public.
Yet, when we come to deal, as we must, with trade treaties with other lands wc should put up a united front. We should not in this House be fighting proposals pTO and con and assisting those who are our competitors for the trade of the world by giving them information in that way that they would not otherwise get. We should put up an undivided front to them, and I believe that in the near future we shall have such a board as that which I have suggested to deal with matters that affect us as far as our foreign trade is concerned. In our domestic attairs this does not matter so much. We can meet together here and discuss, I hope in a friendly spirit, all these questions of domestic concern, we can present our views to the public in general. elections as they come around and whatever policy seems to suit the public best will prevail because representatives will be returned to support that policy. But I say again, in regard to our dealing with foreign matters, that we ought to stand shoulder to shoulder on both sides of the House and we ought not to be engaged in unseemly squabbles in regard to matters of very great concern to the people of vns country.
I have taken up the time of the House at much greater length than I had intended, and I have always laid down the doetrme that no individual member should occupy the time of the House at any very great length. I have criticised speeches of four, five, six, seven and eight hours' length that have been delivered in this House, and I hope that I will never be a sinner in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, while I am succeeding the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright) in this debate, I trust he will pardon me if I do not follow him in all the subjects he has discussed during the course of his speech. I merely desire to refer to one criticism which he has directed against the representatives o, the West on mis side of the House. What he said would seem to indi-29
cate that he regarded it as a complaint that the farmers of the West have sent to the House lawyers or other professional men bo represent them. I remember very well	the record of the late
Conservative Government from 1878 to 1896, and during all that time the portfolio of Agriculture was held by a brewer, a lawyer, or a doctor. If our friends in the Conservative party think there is no person qualified to represent the farmers in Canada but farmers-and I recognize that farmers are well able to represent themselves and other interests in the coun-'try-and if our Conservative friends think it is a reflection upon the farmers of Canada that they should be represented by professional men, I want to know how it was that a Conservative Government during all these years did not find any farmers in Canada to take the portfolio of Agriculture, but, as I stated a moment ago, placed at the head of the Agricultural Department a brewer, a doctor and a lawyer. These men were all very good in their way, but if the argument of my hon. friend from Muskoka should prevail, then I think he would be able to express the same opinion of his own party in the House. It remained for the Liberal Government from 1896 to 1911 to place the first farmer in Canada in charge of the portfolio of Agriculture. As I said, I do not propose to follow my hon. friend any further.
For the second time in a period covering a little over six months we are called together for the purpose of discussing matters pertaining to the greatest war known in history and to provide for Canada's participation in support of British arms. At the extraordinary meeting of Parliament in August last, which continued for the short period of five days, by unanimous vote, we supplied this Government with a war credit of $50,000,000 besides passing other legislation incidental thereto. Since that date we have witnessed the splendid response made by Canadians to the call of Lord Kitchener for " men and more men." From every city, town and hamlet, from the far North to the American boundary, from Cape Breton to Prince Rupert, there have been gathered companies, brigades, battalions and contingents of which it was our pleasure the other day to view the very climax and culmination in the magnificent body of men contributed by British Columbia to the overseas forces.

statement that forty-four thousand settlers in Canada had returned to the United States is correct.
One other instance I desire to refer to, and that is the conduct of the Government in relation to the reduction of the cement duties in 1912. During the session of 1913, the right hon. leader of the Opposition called the attention of the Government to the correspondence which had appeared in the newspapers some months before in which a gentleman in the city of Toronto, a supporter of the Government, had bitterly complained, that, notwithstanding that the Government had given him, or the interest in which he was concerned,
5 p.m. a distinct and specific promise that the cement duty would not be interfered with, that duty had actually been reduced fifty per cent, leaving the manufacturers of cement for the moment in an embarrassed position. An election took place in Saskatchewan about the time of this reduction and the question of cheaper cement, as well as cheaper goods of all kinds necessary for the settlers of the West, was a question which specially occupied the minds of the electors at that time. It was thought that by cutting the duty on cement some advantage might be gained by the Conservative party in that election, and notwithstanding that the Prime Minister a few weeks before, had given his *solemn assurance to this cement manufacturer that the cement duty would not be [DOT]interfered with, this cut of fifty per cent was made. This friend and supporter of the Government wrote a letter in which he protested against that conduct. He said: When I received your letter on the subject of the cement duty, I got the authority of my directors to spend a considerable sum in enlarging our plant and increasing our output, but we have been so embarrassed by the situation arising that we have lost our money and our shareholders will not hereafter have the confidence in the Government with respect to trade matters that they would otherwise have had.
During all the years when the Liberal party was in power, I believe, there never was an interference * with the tariff by Order in Council except in one instance. When the late Minister of Finance intended to change the tariff, he made his announcements first in the House of Commons, and they were accepted only after full and thorough debate, and in this way the public was kept informed of what was likely to take place in respect of tariff changes. But in this instance there was mo discussion in Parliament, no notice of

the action to be taken by the Government; the stroke came like a bolt from the blue; with the result that the confidence of business men in this Government received a shock from which it has not recovered.
So, if we have bad times in Canada, if there has not been in some respects as great an output of production or as much employment as we might have expected, the conditiori may be attributable to the fact that the business community in Canada have not the confidence in this Government that they had in its predecessor.
I would like to discuss another matter which relates to the Civil Service situation. A statement was brought down in the House a few days ago in which it was disclosed that between the time the present Government came into power and March, 1914, something like two thousand civil servants had been dismissed and their places taken by something over ten thousand. The Prime Minister in the course of a speech delivered in Halifax before the election of 1911, made this statement:
A government holds the power of patronage for the benefit of the public, and it is entitled to fill public offices solely in the public interest. The duties of those officials are for the public benefit and are fixed by the laws of the country; their salaries are paid out of the people's money. To use the power of filling such positions as a reward for party service and without regard to the character and capacity of the individual selected is a gross breach of a solemn public trust. A private trustee so dishonouring his office would be subject to punishment by the criminal law, but the one punishment which can be meted out for such abuse of a public trust is dismissal by the electorate.
We have had a revelation made within the last few days which is very startling in view of the source from which it comes; I have before me a statement by Professor Shortt, the chairman of. the Civil Service Commission, dealing with this matter. In an address which he recently delivered in the city of Ottawa he said:
" Patronage is entirely and absolutely in control of the lower grade appointments in the Civil Service," declared Professor Adam Shortt, Chairman of the Civil Service Commission, addressing the People's Forum last night. "Seven out of every nine appointments have patronage behind them."
"There have been many promotions in salary even where there were no vacancies in the upper ranks," he said. " The Civil Service is therefore in the same condition of an army with too many officers. The British expert, Sir George Murjiy, was shocked when he noticed this condition, and I am sick and tired of asking the Government to remedy this state of affairs.
" It is no use arguing that the high cost of living makes these salary promotions necessary; everybody has to pay for the necessaries of life, but not all get promotions. .. I have

met men In the Canadian Civil Service," he said, " who, though they held positions under the Government, were quite ready to admit that the Civil Service system was rotten."
Now, when this Government came into power they made loud professions as to the manner in which they would deal with the Civil Service. We have heard a great deal during the last few months on the subject of " Patriotism and Production." I believe that a distinguished philosopher once said that the greatest patriot was he who caused two blades of grass to grow where only one flourished before.
That principle is applied by the present Government in a somewnat. different manner. Their patriotism consists in patriotism for their party alone, their production consists in producing five government officials where only one flourished before. We have many instances of this kind of patriotism and production. We have the instance, brought up in the House of Commons a few days ago, where a customs official in my county was dismissed by the Minister of Customs because it was alleged that there was nothing for him to do; thereupon the minister appointed another official to do that nothing, at a salary of $250, being $150 more than his predecessor had received.
The man we appointed has been doing something since his appointment; the other man did not do anything.

I would like to get the record from the department of what the man is doing at the present time, and I take this opportunity of requesting the hon. minister to lay a report to that effect on the table of the House.
In the province of Nova Scotia a man was appointed in the Department of the Interior to discharge certain duties, his jurisdiction extending over the maritime provinces. For five or six years he discharged his duties to the satisfaction of the department and its officials. But there was in the city of Halifax a young man, secretary of the Conservative Association of that city, who desired to obtain employment in the public service. For some time he was not given a position, and he became very insistent. It was necessary to provide a position for him, and in the month of October last the officials of the Department of the Interior appointed him at a salary of $1,800 a year-with expenses and office allowance, amounting to $2,500- to assist the other officer to discharge the dutieswhich he himself was quite capable of performing. Whatever extenuation there may
have been in the past, when times were good, revenues bounteous and surpluses large, for the Government is indulging in extravagances of that kind, there is surely no excuse at a time when it is necessary, owing to financial conditions, for a Minister of Finance to issue phoney money from the printing machines in the form of Dominion notes issued without authority and without the necessary gold reserve.
Permit me to cite another instance which occurred in the county of Richmond, and which was dealt with in this House a few years ago. It was necessary for the Department of Railways and Canals to expropriate lands for the improvement of the St. Peter's canal. The owner of the land, a friend of this Government, was a defeated candidate on several occasions in that county. The Department of Railways and Canals paid him about $1,000 an acre for the land that was required from him. It appeared in evidence in tins House that the land had been purchased by him a few years before for $10.50 an acre, and that subsequent to that his property had been assessed at $75 an acre. He moved in the Supreme Court to have the assessment quashed on the ground that the valuation was excessive. In evidence read (before the court he proved tihat the property was not worth $75 an acre, and in this evidence he was supported by certain leading citizens of the town in which I live. That was about three years before he sold the land to the Government. When the property was expropriated by the Department of Railways and Canals, they appointed three commissioners, resident in the town, to value that property. Two of these commissioners were two of the gentlemen who swore three years before that the property was not worth $75 an acre, and the third was the campaign manager of the defeated candidate in the previous election. These three men awarded the owner of the property a valuation of $1,000 an acre, notwithstanding the fact that that valuation was far above and beyond any value which attached to the property. This was an instance where over $3,000 was given to a party friend for the purpose of discharging a party obligation. It does appear to me that the whole resources of this Government are being exploited for party advantage, and for party advantage only.
I could give other reasons why we have_ a deficit of some $60,000,000 at the present time. When the Minister of Finance delivered his speech before the Commercial Travellers' Association in the city of Montreal, perhaps

he njig'M be excused if he did not fully appreciate the indications of the. far-reaching depression which was about to become prevalent throughout the Dominion of Canada. The Finance Minister's mature years were co-incident with that happy period in Canada from 1896 to 1911 when the Liberal party was in power and when there were no such things as hard times, scarcity of money, deficits, or trade depression. But his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce well knew what these signs portended. During all the years that he was Finance Minister in the Conservative Government which was defeated in 1896, hard times and unemployment supped, dined and lodged with him. He was nevei free from the glowering shadows of those unwelcome spectres; they were unbidden guests at every cabinet council and at every party caucus. The Minister of Trade and Commerce well knew what these things forebode, and if the hon. Minister of Finance was not in a position properly to appreciate the conditions which were upon us, it is unfortunate that he did not consult his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
At the session of Parliament of 1913 the minister brought down certain proposals with regard to the supplies for that year. No attempt was made during that sessiou to meet the stringency which was about to bear upon our commercial conditions. There was a period between 1896 and 1911 when there were evidences that the great expansion and prosperity which Canada had tHeretofore enjoyed were about to be checked for a period. In the Budget speech delivered on March 17, 1908, by the Hon. W. S. Fielding, then Finance Minister, he said:
Business has received a check but do not look for a continued period of depression. On the part of the Government it is a time for caution. Large new enterprises which would call for great outlay will be laid aside for a little while.
lhat was the position Mr. Fielding took in 1908, and in 1909, when he was bringing down the Estimates for that fiscal year, he gave further proof of his preparation for the expected depression. Referring to his Budget speech delivered in that year, he said:
With this condition of revenue and with the very many demands made upon us, it would almost seem unavoidable that we should meet the difficulties by an increase in taxation. In some other countries that seems to be the remedy for the financial conditions that have there arisen. In our judgment, however, there is no need here of increased. taxation. "We 
think the truer and sounder method is to meet the situation by a substantial reduction in our expenditure, and that is the method we have adopted. Unquestionably if we were to continue the same rate of expenditure as that which has prevailed in recent years, we should he obliged to add to the burdens of taxation; hut we have come to the conclusion that the part of wisdom is to ask all concerned to be patient with us for the time while we put the brakes severely on expenditure.
That is the attitude taken by Hon. Mr. Fielding at a time when no person in a position to judge of the financial conditions then existing thought that apything like such a severe depression was upon us as was upon the present Finance Minister during the session of 1914. Further on Mr. Fielding said:
We know that in many parts of the country) great works are projected, railways, canals!, and other enterprises, which might in themselves be worthy enough, some of which will have to be undertaken at a later date and; will figure largely in the development of Canada ; but it Is much more important that we>
should, in the present condition of affairs, await an improved financial condition. Therefore we say to the promoters of all these enterprises, no matter how worthy they may be, that they must he content to let them stand' aside for the present.
What was the condition of affairs in 1914? In 1914 there was every appearance of distress at the time that Parliament was opened for the session of that year. Words were placed in the mouth of His Royal Highness the Governor General, which I read a few moments ago, and which indicated that the Government was not unaware that a serious condition of affairs threatened this whole country. But the present Finance Minister did not take the steps followed by his predecessor in the year of which I spoke. In 1909-10 Mr. Fielding reduced the expenditure upon consolidated fund account by $9,334,243. He reduced it upon capital account by $13,247,215, making a total reduction of his Estimates from the preceding year of $22,581,458. It is quite true that at the end of the fiscal year it was found that he had not maintained that decrease; but why? Because the equilibrium of the revenue had been established in the meantime, and there was every indication that a revenue almost equal to that of the preceding year, would be enjoyed by the treasury during the years 1909 and 1910, but, notwithstanding the expenditure, that year was in fact $5,000,000 less than that of the preceding year, but Mr. Fielding still had a surplus that year of $22,091,963. The hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Mac-donell) endeavoured to take some credit for the Government because in the Estimates for the present year it is proposed to reduce

them by a considerable sum of money. In giving a list of reductions in the expenditures for 1915-16, as compared with those for 1914-15, he read items to the House which aggregated the sum of $17,780,320. This, you will remember, is for the year 1915-16, but these reductions did not apply to the last year. In answer to my hon. friend from South Toronto, all I can say is that if the foresight of the Government was only equal to its hindsight, the Finance Minister would not have a deficit of $60,000,000 by a blooming sight. But it is not in 1915-16 that they should have reduced their expenditure, it was in 1914-15. If the Finance Minister had done so, then we would not now be met with the condition of affairs which was disclosed by his Budget statement.
I have here a statement which has been brought down to the House to-day showing the expenditures from month to month during the years 1912, 1913 and 1914. I shall take the expenditure for the last three months of 1913 and the last three months of 1914 and see to what extent the Finance Minister was preparing to meet the financial obligations which were maturing and which have been disclosed in the Budget speech. In September 1913, the expenditure on consolidated revenue account amounted to $9,268,518.33. For the corresponding month in 1914, when the war was on and with every sign of the financial depression and the scarcity of money apparent on all sides, he increased that expenditure to $12,962,824.66. The capital expenditure for September, 1913, amounted to $3,892,564.02 and in September 1914 to $4,581,282.73. Special expenditure in September 1913 amounted to $80,145.02. In September 1914 it amounted to $687,201.81.
In October 1913, the expenditure on consolidated fund account amounted to $8,749,737.11. In October 1914 it amounted to $9,696,064.71. The capital expenditure in October 1913 was $3,343,026.36 and in October 1914 it was $4,479,119.80. Special expenditure for October 1913, amounted to $3,673,060.02 and for October 1914 $84,057.76.
In November, 1913, the consolidated fund expenditure was $9,232,141.30 and in November, 1914, it was $10,496,923.83. The capital expenditure in November, 1913, was $4,231,379.18 and in November, 1914, it was $4,250,385.75. Special expenditure for November, 1913, was $2,068,074.11 and for November, 1914, $350,245.68.
In December, 1913, the consolidated fund expenditure was $9,308,955.66 and in December 1914, it was $9,942,985.96. The capital expenditure in December, 1913, was $3,407,611.33 and in December, 1914, it was $2,910,167.25. The special expenditure in December, 1913, was $797,683.49 and in December, 1914, it was $1,532,807.78.
We have here a record which certainly does not indicate care and forethought on the part of the Finance Minister. The total increase during the four months, September, October, November and December, 1014, as compared with the same months of 1913 amounted to $3,686,188. We have certainly no indication in these figures that the Finance Minister, even as late as December 1014, realized that there was reason for economy. But how is it proposed that the deficit shall be met? It is proposed that this deficit on ordinary expenditure and on capital account, apart from the war, shall be met by certain special-taxes as well as by increases in the tariff rates. For the extravagance that I have pointed out-and I have only pointed out a few isolated cases-the people of Canada will be compelled, while the present Government is in power, to pay an extra cost on nearly every necessity of life as well as special taxes on other things which will add materially to the burden of the cost of living. We have increased duty on bananas, against which a very loud protest has been raised throughout this country, wearing apparel, boots and shoes, many kinds of foodstuffs, drugs and many other products which enter into the daily consumption and the ordinary business of almost every consumer in the Dominion of Canada. Somefewyears ago, and after the present Government came into office, the fishermen of the maritime provinces demanded a change in the interpretation of the tariff with respect to the duty on cotton twine used in the manufacture of lobster traps. The interpretation which had been placed upon it previous to the change of Government was regarded as too liberal for the fishermen, inasmuch as the actual commodity used in the construction of lobster traps was not described in the tariff. The result of the new interpretation put upon that item by the present Minister of Customs was to place upon the tax list an item which for many years under the old Government had been free, with the result that the fishermen of the maritime provinces have had to pay a higher price for that commodity ever since. In the session of 1912, I called the attention of the Minister of Finance to this unfairness, and he was good enough to say

that at the next revision of the tariff he would look into the matter. The next amendment to the tariff was made in the session of 1913, and while several articles heretofore taxed were placed on the free list by the tariff amendment of that year, notably coarse thread which is used by manufacturers of thread in certain cities in the province of Ontario, the Finance Minister did not see his way clear to reduce the duty upon this twine used by the fishermen, and as a consequence they have had to pay the duty ever since. So that in addition to the duty of 25 per cent heretofore collected by the present Government upon this kind of twine, there is to be an additional duty of 7i per cent, and the fishermen of the maritime provinces will be obliged to pay that additional tax to make up for the deficit of the Minister of Finance -a deficit which is due to the wanton and unjustifiable extravagance of the several departments of this Government.
There is another item in which the fishermen of the maritime provinces are interested, and that is corkwood. Ever since 1897, corkwood has been on the free list. By the revision of the tariff made in 1897 by the Minister of Customs of that day and his associates, corkwood and many other things necessary in the prosecution of the fisheries were put on the free list. I notice that in the list made by the Minister of Finance of articles which will not be affected by the proposed increase of 7i per cent, there is no mention of corkwood; so that necessarily this important item, hitherto free, will be taxed. If it is not too late, I most earnestly request the Minister of Finance to look into this matter, and inasmuch as nearly all the other articles used by fishermen in the prosecution of their industry are upon the free, list perhaps the Minister of Finance might see his way to put corkwood on the free list, as it was before.
What is to be the consequence of the increase in the tariff? Is it to be a temporary or a permanent increase? For my part I think there are signs and indications that the present increases are to be regarded as a permanent institution. The interests that have been able to get this advantage over the consumers of Canada are not likely to yield it up very readily. We know the history of the United States with respect to tariff. We know that the American Civil War was the excuse for imposing high protective duties in that country. Large obligations were incurred by the

United States Government during the Civil War, and as a consequence the duties had to be very largely increased. We know how the consumers of that country have struggled ever since to get the tariff reduced. We know that from 1865 up to the year 1913 they did not succeed in securing any decrease whatever. The interests that had grown up under the new tariff came forward year after year urging that the tariff be retained, and the consequence was that in a few years the United States had the highest tariff that has ever been imposed in any country. A writer of that day said of this tariff:
A system of taxation more comprehensive, more burdensome and more confused than it has ever been the lot of any other civilized community to hear.
Further on he says:
The tariff of 1864 is the real war tariff, andj the basis of the present tariff. While the main reasons of its passage were without doubt the need of increased revenue for the Government and the desire to compensate the various interests for the burdens imposed on them by the internal revenue, it is undeniable1 that its final shape was largely owing to the! endeavours of the protected manufacturers toi gain each for himself the greatest possible advantage irrespective of the other's interests. Above all, the habits engendered during this period of comprehensive protection to every thing led to a crystallization of the sentiment1 in favour of national exclusion and isolation. The commercial policy of the United States for many decades was moulded by the dealings and habits generated during the period of the civil war. Henceforth the move-' ment in favour of high protection, which still! in great part dominates the American people, was to become the leading feature in the commercial and political life of the country. What was in its origin a mere temporary expedient called forth by the exigencies of a great military struggle was to become a permanent institution.	I
We have had our first war tariff in Canada. We had the first instalment of it in August, 1914, and we are now getting the second instalment. There would be some excuse for asking the people of Canada to bear the burden of an increased tariff if these were actually war taxes, but in view of the facts that are well known throughout of the country at the present time and of the facts that have been made known in this House since this debate began, it is inconceivable and incomprehensible how the Minister of Finance can bring down a tariff for the purpose of raising ordinary revenue and call it a war tariff, and blame the war for the necessity of bringing it on. The Minister of Finance is largely interested in important financial corporations

in Canada, and he is certainly not without familiarity with corporation law. Let me ask him what would happen if the president or general manager or board of directors of a corporation in Canada were to put shares upon the market and ask for subscriptions to funds to be applied on capital account or for the purpose of increasing the capital outlay of that corporation, and who then, notwithstanding the statement in the prospectus, applied those funds for the purpose of paying salaries.
I am quite sure that a board of directors that would do such a thing would very soon be brought into intimate relationship with the crown attorney and with the judge presiding over the criminal court. In any other walk of life that would not be tolerated. I am bound to say it is absolutely improper and indefensible to couple a demand for war revenue with increased taxes which are required only for the purpose of paying the ordinary expenditure of the country.
There is another tax imposed upon the people by this tariff which will be- extremely irksome and annoying. I refer to the postage tax. Now, if it is necessary for the Government to resort to this mode of taxation, why do they not as a matter of principle raise the postage on letters to three cents and on postal cards to two cents? That would have been very much better, and much less annoying than the present scheme. I am familiar with conditions existing in the country. We know that the owner of a farm, for instance, does not waste his time running to and from the post office. Neither do the grownup members of his family, for they are employed in more important and serious work. The duty of carrying letters to and from the post office devolves upon the younger members of the family. Heretofore, when a farmer wanted to post a letter, he gave his child two cents, and he went to the post office, bought the stamp, placed it on the envelope and posted the letter, which then went on to its destination. What is the reason for the complicated system the Finance Minister proposes? There are going to be difficulties and irritations without end.
The child going to the post office after the new tariff is in force will have to ask not only for a two cent stamp, but in addition the one cent tax stamp which will also have to be attached to the letter, and if, through the ignorance or illiteracy of the postmaster, an ordinary one cent stamp is
placed upon the letter instead of the tax stamp, the letter will find its way into the dead letter office, or the receiver of the letter will be penalized to the extent of double the deficiency in postage. I intimated that there was such a thing as illiterate and incompetent postmasters in this country. Perhaps it will come as a surprise to you, Mr. Speaker, to know that the term "illiteracy" could be properly applied to functionaries occupying the responsible office of postmaster, but it is a fact that under the present Government there have been appointed postmasters who are absolutely illiterate, and are unable to read the directions upon the letters coming into their charge, or to know the denominations of the ordinary postage stamps. There is a case in my own county where a postmaster was dismissed. He was competent, and he had discharged his duties as such for a good many years. There was no fault to be found with him. After the change of Government a complaint was made that he was a Liberal, and his office was removed to a neighbouring house. He received his notice of dismissal, and he was directed to hand over the property of the Postoffice Department to his successor. His successor came to the postoffice, a list was made out of the articles belonging to the Postoffice Department, and the retiring postmaster passed his successor oyer a receipt for those articles and asked him to sign it. The successor said: I can not sign it. The retiring postmaster said: Why can you not sign it? And his successor replied: Because I am not able to read or write. The postmaster stated: You will not get the property until you sign for it. The new postmaster had to go to the nearest village and get into communication with the postmaster there. The postmaster there telegraphed the postoffice inspector at Halifax, and the inspector at Halifax instructed the postmaster at the neighbouring village to go to the postmaster who had been dismissed and sign the receipt for the new postmaster. That is not a fanciful tale, but it is in line with many of the appointments which are being made by this Government. We have food inspectors appointed who can not tell the difference between a porterhouse steak and a gad of smelts, and we have fruit inspectors appointed who do not know the difference between a Gravenstein apple and a Brussels 'sprout. These are conditions which have grown up under the present Government, notwithstanding the fact that these hon. gentlemen, while, in opposition, decried 'long and loud the system of patronage as it had developed during that period.

But we have other things which we are interested in and which we will continue to think about from time to time as a result of this new tariff. Upon the delivery by the Finance Minister of Ms Budget we had a deputation of two hundred tobacco growers from Ontario and Quebec asking to have more protection upon their tobacco. If every industry in Canada is to be protected I would, like to know why the tobacco growers are not to be able to enter the swim as well as others. If they do not get what they ask for it must be because they are not organized and are not an adjunct of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. The Budget of the Finance Minister is an announcement that this is a protectionist Government and that protection not only for revenue but protection to prohibit the importation of foreign goods of any description is to be their policy. The amount of revenue that we will derive from the new Budget proposals of the Finance Minister remains to be seen when the tariff proposals are taken up in Committee of the Whole House. It would, I am sure, be interesting to inquire what amount of revenue can be derived under the proposals of the Government in respect to many of these tariff increases; but apart from the additional burdens which are to be placed upon the people by this increase of the tariff, there are annoyances and disagreeable features that ought to be remedied and which, if not remedied, will lead to the utmost confusion/

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to several addresses which have been delivered on this Budget, although I did not have the opportunity of being present when the main Opposition critic (Mr. A. K. Maclean) delivered his speech.
I have read his speech quite carefully, and notwithstanding the criticisms made by the hon. gentleman and those who have followed him on that side of the House, I can sincerely offer my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) my hearty congratulations on the presentation of his Budget. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Kyte) found some fault with the present Administration for not having appointed, as he said, a farmer as Minister of Argriculture; and he took some credit to the previous Administration for having appointed the Hon. Sydney Fisher, a farmer, as Minister of Agriculture. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Sydney Fisher may have been a farmer, 
but I venture to say that no man ever occupied the position of Minister of Agriculture who had a smaller regard for the farmers of Canada than had the Hon. Sydney Fisher. The Hon. Sydney Fisher, from his place in this House, stated as a reason why the farmers preferred to raise hogs rather than sheep was that the obstinacy of the hog induced the farmer to engage in the production of pork rather than in the production of mutton. He also stated from his place in this House that the farmers were a slip-shod, lazy and indifferent class of people. He is on " Hansard " as having made such a statement, and yet the hon. member for Richmond gives credit to the Liberal Administration for having appointed as Minister of Agriculture a person of that kind.
I was very much amused by some of the arguments advanced by the hon. gentleman, particularly his argument in regard to the extra stamp to be placed on post cards and letters. The hon. gentleman was hard up for an argument when he said that the placing of an extra war stamp on a post card or letter would make the system a very embarrassing one. He said that children who now were sent to the post office by their parents with two cents to buy a postage stamp to put on a letter down in his constituency would hardly be able to handle the extra financing of one cent entailed by putting another stamp on the letter. If we take that as an illustration of the people generally in the county of Richmond we can readily understand how it is that they have their present representative in the House of Commons at Ottawa, but I think the hon. gentleman in making that statement has cast an unwarranted reflection on the intelligence of the people of Richmond.
The intelligence of the Tory postmasters.

I think that, notwithstanding what he says, the people in Richmond will be able to handle this large financial problem and work it out successfully so that letters will not go to the dead letter office. The hon. gentleman has said that during the year 1914 there had been considerable depression and that there were men out of work. That is undoubtedly true. Let us ask why that is the case. The Canadian Pacific Railway Lake Shore line, the Canadian Northern Railway, Ontario division, the Canadian Northern Railway Ottawa-Torcntc branch and several other lines of railway have been completed lately,

throwing out of work men engaged in their construction. I take issue with the hon. member when he argues that at such a time we should put on the brakes at once and stop our public works. It is no time to do that when men are out of employment.
Is it a fact that we on this side of the House are entirely responsible for conditions in Canada at the present time, or is it not the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite should bear the blame? The hon. member said that this new tariff was imposed simply to meet the extravagance of the present Administration. Will the hon. gentleman declare that his party has no responsibility for any of the public works which were started when the Liberals were in power and which had to be completed by the present Government since it came into power? It is a fact that during the last four years ending March, 1915, the Minister of Finance has had to finance some $56,000,000 for the National Transcontinental railway, some $10,000,000 for the Quebec bridge, some $38,000,000 in connection with the extravagant implementing clause of the Grand Trunk Pacific bond issue, for which this Government is not responsible, and some $15,000,000 loaned to the Grand Trunk Pacific. That makes a total of about $120,000,000, for which the Minister of Finance has had to finance. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to be fair, they will not and cannot claim that the present Government is responsible in the main for these necessary expenditures.
Allow me to refer for a moment to some statements made bj previous speakers in regard to Government dismissals. They allege that in the various departments officials of the Government have been dismissed and others have been put in their places. If I have any fault to find with the present Government along that line, it will be because it has not dismissed enough of them. There are a great many more who still retain their positions who should have been dismissed. What is the record of the Liberal party when it came into power in 1896? The. axe fell, and it fell frequently. In the first nine months of the Laurier Administration, 466 Government officials were dismissed without the shadow of an investigation. I am not going to follow all the arguments advanced by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) with regard to this, but I will refer to one or two departments to which he has alluded. Take for instance the Customs Department. The revenue from customs for 1911 was about two and a half
times as much as it was in 1896. The cost of collection advanced by 162 per cent in that time. In 1913, the revenue had increased from $73,000,000 to $115,000,000, or an increase of 57 per cent, while the cost of collection had increased by about 47 per cent. The inward entries in the Customs Department in 1896 amounted to only 528,489, and the outward entries to 104,660. The business had grown enormously during the Laurier regime and continued to grow after the Borden Government took office until in 1913 the inward entries amounted to 1,902,155, and the outward entries to 466,122. It is unreasonable for hon. gentlemen to expect that a department, in which the work was growing at the rate which these figures indicate, could go ahead with its work without any increase in the cost or in the number of officials. It is true the number of officials was increased. In 1911, there were 198 officials in the inside service, and in 1915 there were 232-not a very large increase. In the outside service the increase from Otcober, 1911, to January, 1915, was from 2,273 to 3,144. The salaries paid to these officials indicate just the opposite of what has been charged against the Minister of Customs. They indicate that the ptmost care has been used by the minister in that regard. It is true that the cost of living has increased and the salaries of these officials had to increase; but the increase is not so very great, and the average increase throughout has been more than warranted by the increased cost of living.

I have not the figures. Since October, 1911, a number of new offices have been opened. Three chief ports have been opened, three outports have been made chief ports, and 54 new outports and five preventive and collecting stations have been opened. It is all right to refer to the number of officials in a department, but there are places throughout the country where men are doing preventive officer's work and getting possibly $100 or $150 a year, and they are included in the number of customs officials.
