The Post Office Department also came in for some censure from the hon. junior member from Halifax (Mr. Maclean), and it has not escaped the attention of the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte). The figures presented to the House by the hon. junior member for Halifax show that the revenue from the Post Office Department has each year exceeded the expenditure. But the hon. gentleman looks forward very dolefully to the future and predicts a deficit in that department. Suppose there were a deficit in the Post Office Department. I have maintained before in this House, and have no hesitation in stating now that if there is any department of Government that would be justified in having a deficit it is the post office. The money which makes up the revenue of that department is obtained from the people as payment for postage and should be given back to the people in the form of increased postal facilities. In my county, since this administration took office, the people have obtained postal facilities the like of which they never had before. I have in my county over seven hundred miles of rural mail routes, and many other counties have more than that. I estimate that about one-quarter of the population of the county I have the honour to represent are able to get their mails at their very doors. What was the situation before this Government came into power? The situation was this: The Administration of that day seized upon a suggestion made by the right hon. gentleman who leads the present Govern- , ment in favour of rural free mail delivery, and just before the election of 1908 they established one or two rural routes in the province of Ontario. But from 1908 down to 1911, where were rural routes established? I cannot speak for the other provinces, but I
[Mr. Edwards. 1
know that in my own province of Ontario the rural routes were established only where there was suflicient political pull to get them. That is the fact and no hon. gentleman on the other side can deny it. A member who supported the Government of that day could get a few rural routes established in his county, but a county that was not represented by a Government supporter got no consideration whatever. Under the present Administration rural routes have been extended, and are being extended, regardless of the political complexion of the representative of the constituencies. That is an indication of fairness on the part of this Government which the Liberal Government never displayed.

Before six o'clock I was calling attention to the expenditures in connection with the Post Office Department,	which have been
criticised by the hon. member for Halifax. I was pointing out that if in the Post Office Department the expenditure for the last fiscal year was greater than that of 1911, there was ample justification for that expenditure in the improved postal facilities which this Government has given the people of the country districts in various parts of the Dominion.
I had also called attention to the cost of collecting the custom revenue. The hon. member for Halifax asked as to the cost of collection for the present fiscal year. I do not see how the hon. gentleman can reasonably expect to make any point in that regard. I gave the cost of collection for ten years, and showed that in 1911-12 and 1912-13 the cost of collecting the customs revenue under the present Administration was considerably less than the average cost of collecting during the previous seven or eight years under the Liberal Administration. Undoubtedly during the present year, and possibly during the coming year, there will be an increase in the cost of collecting, because of a loss of revenue, which is inevitable. But I scarcely think that hon. gentlemen opposite would argue that the moment your revenue begins to fall you should immediately dismiss your officials Tight and left, in order to keep the cost of collecting down to the average cost of previous years. That would be imposing an unnecessary and very unjust hardship upon many officials.

Let me read to the House the words of a former Liberal member of this House in regard to one matter of expenditure for which the" country -holds the Liberal party responsible. I quote from the Winnipeg Tribune, the editor of which is Mr. R. L. Richardson, a former Liberal member of this Parliament. The article, which is headed " Graft and Loot," deals with the Transcontinental Railway scandal, and this is what that gentleman says:
The entire report is such a record of incompetence, and dishonesty, and graft and loot that it ought to be sufficient to sink the country. Just what men like Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. Fielding, Mr. Sifton, Mr. Graham, the then Minister of Railways, must think of the situation, would be Interesting to know. Some of these men are still in public life, and others have retired, but they have certainly bequeathed a legacy to their country which should stand as a monument to their disgrace for the next century or two, until their names shall have rotted in oblivion. The appalling corruption and mismanagement in connection
with this undertaking practically destroys it for all time as an asset to the Dominion. That is the opinion of a former Liberal member of the Government which went out of power when this Government took office -and a Liberal candidate for election since that time-in regard to graft, loot and extravagance. I respectfully commend his words to hon. gentlemen opposite when they feel disposed to talk about the graft and extravagance of this Administration.
It has been stated by the Finance Minister and by the junior member for Halifax- and not denied-that there wild inevitably be an increase in the public debt of Canada. Let us look at the question of the national debt just for a moment. In 1896, the year the Liberal party came into power, the net debt of Canada was $258,497,432. In 1911, when they left office, the net debt was $340,042,052. So that they had succeeded in increasing the debt of Canada by over $81,500,000. The Borden Government took office in October, 1911, and at the end of the last fiscal year, March 31, 1914, they had decreased the net debt by something over $6,000,000. The present fiscal year will see an addition to the deot of Canada, due to Canada's participation in the defence of the Empire we love and of liberties that we hold sacred.
A decline in revenue and an increase in expenditure means, of course, an addition to the national debt; and no matter what party had been in power at the present time, I maintain that an increase in our national debt for this year was inevitable under the circumstances. In that, of course, I am assuming that if the Liberal party had been in power they would have gone on and participated in the present war as we have done. The Finance Minister puts the loss of revenue for the present year at $33,000,000. I would like hon. gentlemen opposite, in criticising the Budget, as they have a perfect right to do, to state how they would have altered or changed the policy of the Dominion of Canada so as to have avoided a declining revenue at the present time. Surely no hon. member in this House will to-day stand up and express the opinion that the adoption of the reciprocity

pact would have prevented the loss in revenue which has taken place. Surely no political party in this or any other country ever had its folly fully brought home as the folly of the Liberal party has been brought home to it in the last twelve months. For . the years 1911-12, 1912-13, 1913-14 the sur-plusses are the largest in the financial history of the Dominion of Canada. We have had heavy expenditures on public works that had to be completed-the National Transcontinental railway, the Quebec bridge, the Hudson Bay railway, the Welland canal-and which of these would the hon. gentlemen opposite have stopped? If I mistake not, the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition not only favoured the construction of the Welland canal, but also favoured entering on the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, and that within the last twelve months. Special taxes are required at the present time to meet special conditions. Will anybody question the correctness of that statement? To meet the necessities of our war expenditures and our pension list, special taxation is necessary. If no war existed these special taxes would not be necessary, and the situation would have been met without difficulty. In regard to expenditure, what has been the record of the Liberal party? I remember that previous to 1896, before they came to power, the Liberal party pledged itself to reduce the expenditure which at the time was $38,000,000 or $40,000,000 a year. This amount they declared to be outrageous; in fact, from one end of the country to the other they declared that the then Conservative party was grinding the people between the upper and the nether millstone of taxation; and that if they were returned to power they would reduce that expenditure by at least several millions. That statement, of course, at that time was just as bad as the statements they are making from their seats on the other side of the House to-day. What was their record when in power? Instead of reducing the expenditure, in the first five years the average ran, not from $38,000,000 to $40,000,000, but over $50,000,000; in the next five years it averaged over $72,000,000, and in the next five years it averaged over $113,500,000, reaching more than $133,000,000 in 1909. They declared they would lessen the taxes of the people. Did they fulfil that pledge? The taxes represented by customs and excise in 1896 amounted to $5.46 per head of the population. In 1906 they amounted to $10 per head of population, and in 1911, still under Liberal rule, to $12 per head of population. That is how 
they kept their pledge to reduce taxation. But Canada's national debt is not to be measured, merely in dollars, and while I submit that the Liberal party in this country is responsible for a very large part of Canada's national debt as represented in dollars, the Liberal party in this country is responsible, I believe I might say entirely responsible, for that part of Canada's national debt which is not measured in dollars, because there is a debt that this country owes, and which under Liberal administration was allowed to accumulate and increase from year to year, a debt of gratitude to the Mother Country, which they never seemed disposed to pay, and which was allowed to accumulate under their administration.
Allow me to call attention for a few moments to our trade. Canada's -imports for the year ending March 31,	1914,
amounted to $635,511,492, which was $31,000,000 less than our imports for the previous year, but notwithstanding that falling off, was $173,500,000 more than our imports in 1911.	In 1914 our exports
of Canadian produce amounted to $431,500,000, which was $75,800,000 more than in 1913 and $157,272,000 more than in 1911.	Canada's total trade
in 1914 showed an increase over 1913 of $34,500,000, and an increase over 1911, the last year of Liberal rule, of $460,300,000. Our trade with France shows a decrease in our imports of a little over $1,000,000 and an increase in our exports to that country of about a like amount. Our trade with Germany for 1914 shows a slight increase in our imports from that country, less than one-quarter of a million, and an increase of over $1,000,000 in our exports to that country. Our imports from the United Kingdom were $6,800,000 less than in 1913, but our exports to the United Kingdom in 1914 were $44,340,000 more than in 1913. To the United States our exports in 1914 were $25,900,000 more than in 1913, and our imports from that country were $39,300,000 less than in the preceding year. Of Canada's exports of animals and their products, 69 per cent go to the British Empire and 31 per 'cent to other countries. Of Canada's exports of agricultural products, 56 per cent go to the British Empire and 34 per cent to all other countries. Seventy-two per cent of our surplus farm products for which we have to find a market go to the United Kingdom, 124 per cent to the United States, and 154 per cent to other countries. In other words 874 per

cent of those surplus products goes across the ocean, and is absolutely dependent upon Britain's supremacy on the seas for its safe conduct to the markets of the world. Let me give an example to illustrate the importance of this. In the first week after the war, salesmen representing various cheese factories in Eastern Ontario and Western Quebec attended their regular cheese board meetings, but were informed by the buyers of big exporting firms in Montreal, that they had had instructions not to buy any cheese that week. The reason given was that the exporting firms of Montreal did not*feel that the trade routes were absolutely safe on account of the war. This was a serious matter for many of the farmers of Eastern Ontario, where dairying is _carried on very -extensively. The incident directed the attention of farmers from one end of the country to the other to the possibility of serious loss on account of the war. If we could not. export our cheese, neither could we export our apples or our wheat. The next week, however, it was cabled to Canada from England that the trade routes were perfectly safe, and that the people of this country could export their produce as usual. What was it that made the trade routes safe? The British fleet. For years, every other overseas dominion had been contributing to the upkeep of that fleet. But the supremacy of Britain on the seas meant more to Canada, and particularly to the farmers of Canada, than it did to the people of any, or perhaps all, of the other overseas dominions; and yet this country, because of the action of the hon. gentlemen opposite, was in the position of being the only one of the overseas dominions that had never contributed a cent to- wards maintaining the supremacy of the British navy.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have often said in the past that the United States is Canada's natural market for wheat, and pretty nearly everything else. I feel that it is incumbent on me to give a few figures to demonstrate, as I think they will, that that argument is absolutely fallacious. Our wheat production in 1913 was something over 231,000,000 bushels. In 1914, it dropped to 158,223,000 bushels. To what was that falling off due? It was due to these three causes: unfavourable weather, less acreage under crop, and a smaller yield per acre. The United States in 1913 produced 763,000,000 bushels, and in 1914, 891,950,000 bushels. Their production last year was very great, and was due to the opposites of the three causes I have just mentioned.
Their increase was due to favourable weather, greater acreage under crop, and a larger yield per acre. Let us look at the exports of wheat. The United States exported in 1912, 61,654,000 bushels; in 1913,
99.500.000	bushels, and in 1914, 173,861,000 bushels. Their exports of wheat flour were
10.621.000	barrels in 1912; 12,278,000 barrels in 1913, and 12,708,000 barrels in 1914. In the face of figures like that, can hon. gentlemen opposite still contend that Canada's natural market for wheat is the United States? It is just as reasonable to say that the natural market for Nova Scotia coal is Newcastle-on-Tyne, and hon. gentlemen opposite must surely admit that. We have a good market for wheat in England, but the market for our western wheat in our eastern provinces of Canada' is almost as good. While we send to England
38.000.	000 to 40,000,000 bushels of wheat a year, we send to Ontario, Queoee, the maritime provinces and British Columbia, over
32.000.	000. bushels; so that these provinces alone furnish us with no small market.
Is the United States a market for our barley? The United States export figures do not indicate it. Last year they exported over 17,000,000 bushels; and as regards oats, while they import a lot, their exports of oats amounted to 25,500,000 bushels more than their imports. Is the United States a market for our horses? Last year Canada sold to the United States 4,618 horses, for which we received $583,000. The same year, the United States sold to Canada 33,718 horses, for which we paid $4,877,000. These figures do not convince me that the United States is a natural market for our horses, as hon. gentlemen opposite have frequently said. Take other products. The United States exports over 21,000,000 dozen of eggs and we import over 15,000,000 dozen; yet hon. gentlemen opposite argue that the United States is the natural market for Canada's eggs. Our exports of butter have dropped down to the vanishing point; we import over 8,000,000 pounds a year, and a large portion of that comes from the United States In this connection, let me say that one of the greatest butter-exporting countries in the world is Denmark, which annually exports over 200,000,000 pounds. When considering the tariff I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite- to bear in mind this fact: that butter brought from Denmark or Liverpool can be laid down in the Montreal market for less than one cent a pound for carriage. It has been claimed that the United States is also the market

for Canadian meats. The United States exports of beef run to over 36,000,000 pounds a year, and of hog products, to over one billion pounds aT year. The United States invaded our home markets last year by sending to us 1,339,000 pounds of beef, nearly 9,000,000 pounds of bacon, 1,500,000 pounds of hams and shoulders, over
9,000,000 pounds of lard, and nearly ten million pounds of pickled pork; or a total of over 31,000,000 pounds of meats, to the value of four million dollars and upwards.
Last session I quoted from the United States official bulletin, to show that the prices of foodstuffs in the United States had not been materially affected by the Wilson-Underwood tariff. Why were the prices not materially affected? Because the importations were not sufficient to potentially affect the large supply in that country. But we must remember that a comparatively small quantity of foodstuffs imported into Canada would materially affect the supply here, and have a very strong effect upon prices. What would be a negligible quantity to the United States in comparison with the vast amount of foodstuffs in that country, would not be a negligible quantity if it were brought into Canada, and as I say, would seriously affect prices. That suggests to me another justification besides those already given by the Minister of Finance for the present increase in our tariff, and it is this. Since war broke out, large quantities of foodstuffs produced in the United States have been shut out of the markets to which they formerly went. For instance, the United States had an export trade of farm products to Germany of over $200,000,000 a year; but the war has stopped that, and, on account of the blockade, unsafe trade routes, and for other reasons, these products have also been shut out from other markets they formerly enjoyed. With these products on their hands, the United States would naturally look to selling them to their nearest neighbours, or wherever they could be most easily disposed of. In o'ther words, they would try to dispose of them in this country. And I maintain that, if there were no other justification for this tariff, there is justification for it in order to prevent the dumping into Canada of the surplus productions of countries which through the war have lost the markets they formerly enjoyed. I am speaking as a protectionist when I make that statement. I make no apology for being a protectionist; I am a protectionist because I believe in the policy of protection. I talk in favour of pro-

tection, and in that respect I am unlike some hon. gentlemen opposite, who, believing in protection just as strongly as I do, for political reasons talk the other way; it all depending on which side of the House they are sitting.
Let us look for a moment at the British preference, about which hon. gentlemen opposite seem to be terribly worked up. They frequently talk as if the idea of the British preference originated in the minds of the Liberal party, arid as if it were their child. But they can not demonstrate that, for it is not true. It is a borrowed idea, just as thousands of the ideas that they claim as their own are borrowed or stolen from somebody else. The Toronto Globe of June 13, 1896, in its report of a speech delivered by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in that city, quotes him as saying:
I agree with him (Sir Charles Tupper) in regard to preferential trade. This is a new idea and one which in itself is fraught with greatness, not only for the Canadian people but for the British Empire at large. And now the principle is proclaimed that there shall be preferential trade within the Empire at large.
That idea of Sir Charles Tupper's was, then, a new one to the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The Globe goes on:
That is to say that England and her colonies should trade upon a footing of preference-over other nations. Imagine what would be the consequences if the products of Canada, the wheat, the barley, the oats, the butter, the cheese, which we are sending to England were to be accepted in the British markets on terms of preference over the products of the United States, of Russia, and all other countries which are competing with us in the market. The advantages are obvious, so obvious that the moment I saw the idea I jumped at it, and immediately declared myself in favour of it.
These are the words of the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier: that when the idea which originated in the mind of Sir Charles Tupper first appeared to the vision of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, he jumped at it. But hon. gentlemen opposite have forgotten the jump, and now claim the idea as their own. Shortly after this, Sir Wilfrid Laurier publicly announced, when he was in England, that he did not want any preference for Canadian farm products in the English market, but that he had given the preference to England without asking for any return. Hon. gentlemen opposite harp a good deal on that, but let us follow this British preference a little further. The intention of the Liberal party was to apply the preference, not merely to Great Britain-they did not intend to follow Sir Charles Tupper's idea along that line- but they intended to offer a preference to other countries besides England and the British Empire. In 1897 they

passed what they now call the British Preference Act. I will read the section of the Act that hears upon this:
An Act to consolidate and amend the Acts respecting the duties of customs; assented to 29th June, 1897.
Section 17 is in these words:
When the custom tariff of any country) admits the products of Canada on terms which, on the whole, are as favourable to Canada as the terms of the reciprocal tariff herein referred to are to the countries to which it may apply, articles which are the growth, produce or manufacture of such country, when imported direct therefrom, may then be entered for duty, or taken out of warehouse for consumption in Canada, at the reduced rates of duty provided in the reciprocal tariff set forth in schedule D to this Act.
Let us see what the Finance Minister of that time said. The Finance Minister took pride in the fact that the preference was open to all countries and that we were not doing anything in particular for Great Britain. Here is what he said about the custom tariff of 1897, as quoted in Hansard of that year:
We do not by our resolution offer anything to Great Britain alone. We make our offer, not to Great Britain, but to every nation that is prepared to accept it. We make it to every country which is willing to establish fair and reasonable trade relations with Canada.
These are the words of Finance Minister Fielding on that tariff. The idea put forth by Sir Charles Tupper had undergone some modification. They introduced their tariff changes along the lines of section 17, but no sooner was the Act passed and put in operation than they found themselves in difficulties with other countries on account of existing treaties. They amended the Act in these words:
On and after the 1st day of August, 1898, section 17 of the said Act shall be repealed and the following shall be substituted therefor :
Articles which are the growth, produce or manufacture of any of the following countries may, when imported directly into Canada from any such country, be entered for duty or taken out of warehouse for consumption in Canada at the reduced rate of duty provided in the British preferential tariff set forth in schedule II to this Act.
I want to give hon. gentlemen opposite a few more figures in regard to this British preference which I thought perhaps would be interesting to them and certainly to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). I do not see him present but I hope he will be here in a few minutes. Of Canada's total imports in 1896, 31 per cent were from Great Britain; in 1908, under Liberal Government, only 27 per cent of our total imports were 30
from Great Britain. In 1896, of the imports coming into Canada free of duty 22 per cent came from Great Britain. In 1908, under Liberal Government, notwithstanding all their talk about the preference, only 17 per cent of the goods coming into Canada free came from England. From the United States the proportion rose from 64 per cent free of duty in 18a6 to 70 per cent in 1908.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have been endeavouring to make capital out of the fact that under the Finance Minister's arrangement of the tariff he is not only increasing the general tariff 7J per cent but he is also increasing the British preferential tariff 5 per cent. Hon. gentlemen do not seem to realize that it is possible to increase the rate of duty and yet a-t the same time increase the degree of preference and that is precisely what is being done here. The Budget of the Finance Minister increases the British preference by 21 per cent relatively to other countries. Let us take a case to illustrate that statement. An article worth $100 comes into Canada from England. A similar article worth $100 comes into Canada from the United States. The duty on the article coming from the United States is 30 per. cent, we will say. This 30 per cent on $100 is $30 that has to be paid on that article. The duty on the article coming from England is 20 per cent and 20 per cent on $100 is $20. The British merchant in that case gets his article worth $100 into Canada foT $10 less than it costs the United States merchant. Take the tariff as changed by the Finance Minister. The duty on the article coming from the United States is 37| per cent while the British tax is 25 per cent. The tariff of 37J per cent on the article worth $100 amounts to $37.50 and 25 per cent off the $100 article coming from England is $25. M you subtract one from the other you will find that the preference to the British merchant is $12.50, whereas it was formerly $10.
I want to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Assiniboia and I am sorry he is not here. In discussing the British preference last night the hon. member for Assiniboia got very tragic. and the insurance companies, tax every one of them, make them pay what money you want, but for heaven's sake keep your unholy and disloyal hands off the British preference. So spoke the hon. member for Assi-niboia. Keep your unholy hands-[DOT]
Disloyal.
Yes.

There is another remark which the hon. member for Assiniboia made and which I, as a member of this House, do not feel like letting pass. He begged us to keep our unholy and profane hands
9 p.m. off the British preference; but the hon. gentleman in the course of his remarks saw fit to throw the taunt of disloyalty at members on this side of the House, mainly in regard to the change in the preferential tariff. What about their loyalty in 1911? What was their position as manifested then by their trade policy? They were perfectly willing at that time to make Canada an adjunct of the United States. I do not impugn their party loyalty not for a moment. The hon. gentleman should not forget the Prince Albert deal.

I did not know you had a deal in Prince Albert, too. I know there are mighty few places you missed, ,and it would be rather surprising if you had overlooked Prince Albert. I am very certain that if my hon. friend had been there it would not have been overlooked.
Now, hon. gentlemen opposite argue as if it were possible to raise the general tariff without raising or changing the British preferential tariff. That is absolutely ridiculous. Surely, if hon. members will consider that matter for a little while they will see the fallacy of that. What would be the effect of such a course? You would simply invite disaster to every concern in Canada. Why? Because you would be forcing your Canadian manufacturer to pay an increase of 74 per cent on his raw material while the raw material would still go into Britain free and their goods would be shipped in here at the old rate. ion of Canada. Hon. gentlemen may talk about this 5 per cent addition to the British preference being disloyal or unfair to England, but they would not get any English statesman or politician to say that, because-and I do not wish to be discourteous -they would have more sense.

That was Hon. Mr. Fielding, then Finance Minister. You do not want any sounder protectionist than this speech shows him to be, do you? Now, follow the history a little further. Under the reciprocity pact the Liberals proposed a reduction from 17J per cent to 15 per cent. At that time the hon. member for Dundas asked the then Finance Minister, Mr. Fielding, if there was to be

any change in the valuation for duty. This was Mr. Fielding's answer:
Our negotiations have not touched the question of valuation; that must be left to the operation of the customs authorities of the two countries.
Why was that question asked by the hon. member for Dundas? The Liberal party had gone up and down this country preaching against the manufacturers and declaring their intention of taking the duty off agricultural implements. They did make a reduction in 1907 from 20 per cent to 174 per cent; then they turned to the manufacturers and said: Do not be alarmed, we will fix this up so that it will not hurt you a bit. We will show the farmers that we have made a reduction from 20 per cent to 17i per cent; we will make them believe that we are going [DOT] to take further steps along that line, but we will simply change the value of a binder for duty purposes from $80 to $100. That is exactly what they did. When the rate of duty under the Conservative Government was 20 per cent the duty on a binder was $16; after the Liberal party got through tinkering with it, the duty on the same binder was $17.50.
Last year the hon. member for Moose-jaw (Mr. Knowles) moved this resolution:
That in the opinion of this House the time has arrived when in the interests of the farmers, and consequently in the interests of the whole of Canada, the duties on agricultural implements should be forthwith removed.
Why was it that the " time had arrived?" Just the difference between here and there; just the difference between the right of Mr. Speaker and the left. So far as the arrival of the time is concerned, that makes all the difference in the world. When hon. gentlemen are on this side of the House the time does not arrive, and they proceed to manipulate the tariff in the way that I have indicated. "But when they get on the other side of the House the " time arrives " for them to endeavour to hoodwink the people. If hon. gentlemen opposite were sincere in their contention that to take the duty off agriculural implements would benefit the farmer, why did they not accept the standing offer from the United States to make farming implements free? It was on the statute books of the United States for years; why did they not accept the proposal? They knew perfectly Well that not one per cent of the people of Canada knew of the existence of that provision; consequently they took the course they did.

During the period from 1909 to 1913 Canada imported from the United States over 21,000 mowers, binders and reapers, valued at nearly $1,500,000. I do not hesitate to say that I would rather see those mowers, binders and reapers manufactured in Canada, giving employment to our Canadian artisans.
Hon. gentlemen on the other side have called attention to the matter of cement.
I do not think there is a quality of cement made that would hold together the conflicting ideas of hon. gentlemen opposite. In 1910 the price of cement in Canada jumped up 40 or 50 cents a barrel. The Liberal party was in power at that time. What did they do? Absolutely nothing; they did not attempt to relieve the situation so far as the farmers were concerned, nor did they shed any tears over ,the farmer because he had to pay 40 or 50 cents a barrel more for his cement. I suppose the time " had not arrived " for a change of ideas. Then they brought up the reciprocity pact, under which they proposed a reduction of li cents a hundred pounds on cement, or 4j cents a barrel. If the reciprocity pact had been carried into effect, the duty on cement coming into Canada from the United States, even after the reduction, would still have been three cents a hundred pounds, or nine cents a barrel higher than the United States duty on cement going into that country from Canada. If they had the interests of the farmers at heart, they might at least have proposed to bring the Canadian duty on cement down as' low as the corresponding duty on the other side of the line-but they made no such proposal. They were on the Government benches at the time, and they did not look at the matter of cement as they look at it now. When it became apparent to this Government after they came into power that there was an apparent combine or merger in the matter of cement, they brought the members of that merger to time by a reduction of the duty on cement, thus showing a practical interests in the farmers of Canada. The hon. member for Assiniboia, in referring to this cement merger, implied, it seemed to me, that the men composing that merger were friends of the Conservative party. If I am not mistaken, the head of that company was and is Senator Edwards, a member of the Liberal party. If that combine is in existence at the present time, I have no doubt that the free trade ideas whieh are floating about on the other side of the
House may reach the Senate and have such an effect upon hon. gentlemen of the Senate that the price of cement may be reduced.
But that is not the only evidence of the inconsistency of hon. gentlemen opposite. ' They made a reduction in the duty on coal oil, and in less than three years they handed back to the coal oil men subsidies to the extent of nearly a million dollars.
So that while on the one hand they were apparently giving the people some benefit, on the other they were turning round and soaking them, so to speak, by the payment of these bounties.
We are face to face with a crisis not only in the history of the Empire but of tms country as forming a part of the Empire.
It has been found necessary to increase the rate of duty in order to produce a revenue to meet the conditions caused by the war. Hon. gentlemen opposite may argue until doomsday, but I am convinced that they cannot get the people to see with them in this matter. I am convinced that they cannot impose upon the people of this country their idea that this is not a war tax. This is a war tax due to our falling revenues, whieh revenues have fallen away because of interference with trade, caused by the war. Across the line the United States, which is not engaged in war, has been seriously affected by the war and has been obliged to take unusual steps to make good its loss in revenue, admittedly due to the war. Our revenue has gone down undoubtedly because of this war, prices have gone up, the consumption of products has decreased and so on. This has all had its effect in bringing about abnormal conditions. These conditions must be met, and are being met by the Government by means of these taxes. I want to be fair to hon. gentlemen opposite and at the same time to say what I honestly think. Hon. gentlemen opposite in one breadth say that they wholeheartedly support the Government in voting ' $50,000,000 or $100,000,000 to carry on the war; but in the very next sentence they do their utmost to oppose the only means at the disposal of the Government to raise money for prosecuting the war. It is in my judgment a roundabout way of showing opposition to the Government in their conduct of this war, a roundabout way and therefore not a very creditable way to hon. gentlemen opposite. They cannot make the people of this country believe that this tax is not made necessary by this war. Not only do the people of Canada believe that,

but they will turn with disgust from men who think to make party capital out of this increased taxation, because the people of Canada are patriotic and loyal and will pay these increased taxes and pay them without murmur. Hon. gentlemen may think they are taking a right course; but from Confederation down to the present time hon. gentlemen have never been known to take the right course on tariff matters, never once. That is the undeniable history of this country, that whenever a tariff issue has come up in Canada the Liberal party has always been on the wrong side, at least the people of this country said they were on the wrong side, they have never seemed to be able to grasp tariff matters. Let me beg of them to consider this past record of theirs and to see if that record should not teach them the lesson to beware of themselves when it comes to the consideration of tariff matters.
I heartily concur in the Budget which the Finance Minister has presented to this House. I believe it will benefit this country in more ways than one. Already evidences of that are apparent. To-day the Montreal Gazette contains this little item:
New Plant at Hamilton-$150,000 to be expended by Horse Shoe Concern.
Hamilton, Ont., February 24.-The United States Horse Shoe Company, of Erie, Pa., it was announced to-day, has selected Hamilton for its Canadian headquarters. The company is said to be the largest manufacturer of horse and mule shoes in the world. It will spend 3 150,000 on a plant here to start with and employ 100 men. Construction work starts at once.
I shall place that beside the quotation I gave a short time ago from the speech of the Hon. Mr. Fielding when discussing the duty on agricultural implements. The two taken together seem to me to indicate that this Government, like other Conservative Governments in the past, is following the proper course in this matter.
Mr. Speaker, I trust my hon. friend and my respected friend from Kingston, because I do respect him with all his faults and idiosyncracies-
May I correct my hon. friend, not Kingston but Frontenac.
What about pensions?

We have no Bill before the House providing for pensions. If any Bill is brought before the House I presume it will take effect next year when ample provision can be made for any pensions. The Government has no idea of what will be required for pensions.
Has the hon. gentleman never seen on the statute books an Act providing for pensions?
There is no Bill yet at all events.
There is.

No, not during this session. There is no amount estimated for pensions. Parliament has not been asked to make any provision for pensions and I sincerely trust it will not be called upon to make any large provision for pensions. I trust that better luck than that will attend our young men who have gone to the front. If the time should come when any large amount must be voted for pensions hon. gentlemen will find members on this side of the House standing side by side with them in voting whatever amount may be necessary. I think it has been demonstrated beyond the possibilities of contradiction that if this Government, since it came into power, had exercised even ordinary prudence with reference to the appointment of officials there would have been saved enough money to pay the interest upon this $100,000,tOO which it is proposed to borrow for at least a year and a half.
I have not that familiarity with the Civil Service that Professor Shortt, chairman of the Civil Service Commission, necessarily
has. He is a gentleman who is in the employ of the Government; he occupies, I presume, a quasi independent position as chairman of that commission; he has made the statement, made it publicly, made it with deliberation that under this Government the appointments to the Civil Service in the lower grades are entirely a matter of patronage and he says that, whereas there have been something like 2,000 dismissals from the Civil Service, there have been some 10,000 appointments, making a difference of some 8,000.

I would like to say that this is a statement that has been repeated so often in this House that hon. gentlemen opposite will possibly be beginning to believe it. No more dishonourable, no more dishonest, no more unfair-
Order, order.

Hear, hear.
Mr. ROGERS-statement was ever made by any man than that.
Will the hon. gentleman repeat that?
I want to say that no more dishonourable, no more dishonest, no more-
Order, order.
Untrue.
Hear, hear.
-statement was ever made by any man-
Order, order.
Will the minister repeat it? I could not hear him.

I have repeated it twice, but I shall be glad to stay here and go on repeating- it if it will be any benefit to my hon. friend. I was referring not to my hon. friend hut to Professor Shortt and in that connection I want to say here and now that no more dishonourable, no more dishonest, no more unfair statement was ever made by any man than that made by Professor Shortt, Chairman of the Civil Service Commission. It is an absolutely untrue statement.

I am sure my hon. friend could hardly hear his own voice when he got to the last sentence and it is delightful to see the way in which hon. gentlemen applaud the minister without hearing him. There is a sort of telepathic communication between the supporters of the Government

and my hon. friend and they take it for granted that whatever he says will be right. That is a very delightful position for the minister to occupy with reference to his party. It is more creditable to the hon. gentleman than it is to the party. Ordinarily one would suppose that a party of intelligent gentlemen, and very excellent gentlemen, would like to hear what the minister has to say and then decide whether it was something that should be applauded. The matter becomes a question at issue between the Minister of Public Works and Professor Shortt. Of course, we have to leave that to be settled between them, but unfortunately for my hon. friend's statement, when he makes this terrible imputation against a man of the high standing and independent position of Professor Shortt, the returns which have been brought down to this House by the Government would seem to justify the statement which Professor Shortt makes.

I am sure my hon. friend does not wish to make an unfair statement. He has surely not read the return himself or he would not venture to make that statement. The return shows nothing of the kind. Take the return of my own department for instance; in it 507 dismissals are credited and there are 700 odd resignations which Professor Shortt never takes into account. The same is true of every department of the Government which makes the fact absolutely clear as against Professor Shortt's statement.
We will find out more about that another day.

I shall be very glad to
make my statement good.

I am glad to accept the statement of my hon. friend so far as that matter comes within his own knowledge, but I would suppose that a gentleman of Professor Shortt's standing would not make such a statement without very good foundation.
It is only a partial return.

I base the statement
which I have made, namely, that this is not a war tax, upon the Estimates presented to the House, and I find that one of the necessities for imposing that tax is the very large amount required for the Department of Public Works and for the Department of Railways. I make this assertion, which the Estimates confirm,

namely, that some $18,000,000, which was voted last year for these two purposes, was not required and was not expended; and that notwithstanding the war, notwithstanding the necessity which ought to influence every prudent man in dealing with expenditures, in these two departments alone the Government is asking Parliament to vote $1,000,000 more than was expended during the year 1914-15. That could be justified only upon the ground that they are public works of such an urgent character that there can be neither a postponement nor a reduction in regard to them. That would be an extraordinary condition so far as Government works are concerned, when we know that all the cities and towns in Canada have found it necessary to reduce public works, works on street improvements, work of installation or enlargement of water systems, work in connection with the improvement of the fire department and of the various civic services. Those who govern those cities all feel that in view of the depression, in view of the fact that every man, woman, boy, and girl in this country is doing what he or she can, and is giving his or her mite, little though it may be, towards the various charities	which have	beenorganized in connection with the war, some for the	Red Cross,	some
for the Belgian fund, some for the patriotic fund, some for the hospitals, all doing their part, this is not the time to impose further burdens upon the tax-payers, and that these services ought to be carried over for another year at all events to see whether or not the war is over and whether times may not become (better. Notwithstanding that this is the example which has been set by all the municipalities throughout this vast Dominion, we find this Government asking Parliament for an appropriation for these two services, public works and railways, of $1,000,000 more than it found it possible to expend during the year about to close. I prove that by taking the Estimates which have been laid before Parliament. The re-votes are given in every case so far as the railways and public works are concerned. In the columns giving the votes for 1914-15, the items include not only the main estimates but the supplementary estimates as well, that is, the whole expenses for the current year which will expire on March 31. If we go over these Estimates, item by item, we shall find that a very large number of them are re-votes for harbours and railways; and taking out the ne-votes, we shall find that the Government are asking Parliament to vote $1,000,000 more1 than it

was able to expend during the current year. There are scores of Estimates in these items, some for public works, some for harbour works, in regard to which no contracts have been let and for which it is not intended by the minister-to let the contracts during the coming year. They are put in here-I shall not say to pad the Estimates, but in order to keep these amounts before Parliament and the people of the country, so that when the appropriate time arrives, the minister may engage upon the work and ask for tenders and let the contracts.
Did you ever do that?

Yes. I have often done that, and every minister who has ever been in a government in Canada has done it, and there is no harm in it when conditions are normal. I always kept such items in, because, Parliament being committed to the work, even though it were postponed for two	or three	years, there
was less difficulty in getting the amount voted when it was really necessary to carry on the work. That has been done over and over again. But if. my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works will take us into his confidence and go through these large items, he will agree with me that it will be impossible for him to expend within fro,000,000 or $zO,000,000 of the amount which the Government has put into the Estimates and for which it has asked the approval of Parliament. To meet that ostensible deficiency of $18,000,000 to $2u,-000,000, the Government is imposing this war tax upon the people of this country. That is absolutely unreasonable and unfair, and it is a course which will not commend itself to the good judgment of the people of Canada.
My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works says: Well, what will you do with regard to the public works at St. John? Would you be willing to permit a reduction in the amount to be expended there? I would not be worthy of my position as a member of this House if I did not answer " Yes " to that question. I would not be worthy of the confidence of the people of my constituency if I were so cowardly that I would not dare to stand up in my place ana give an answer to that question in the affirmative. Therefore I say that in these times of stress and trouble the amount proposed for St. John harbour of $1,500,000 might very well be cut down during this year to $750,000. The work could go on, and
a great deal of work could be done for that money.
With regard to Halifax there is an appropriation of $3,000,000. If that were reduced to $1,500,000, a magnificent amount of work could be done there. When we come to the Hudson Bay railway and the terminals at Port Nelson, while I have always been in favour of the construction of that railway, yet we ought to pause, and instead of proposing to expend, as the Government is doing, $5,000,000 during this year on that railway and terminals, the Government ought, in fairness to the people of Canada cut that amount down to the sum of not more than $1,000,000.
There is $4,000,000- which they propose raising by putting a tax upon all people so far as they can reach them and which they propose to spend on this railway away to the north, going through a country where there are no people, going to a harbour where there are no people, and intended to develop a trade which under the conditions now existing is not likely to come for a number of years; and proposing to do it at a time when two of the great transcontinental railways which hav.e been built for the purpose of carrying the traffic between the East and the West, between the interior and the seaboard are almost-and I am speaking now only of what is well known-are almost on the eve of bank- _ ruptcy. They propose to construct that' railway and those terminals immediately, though there is no traffic in sight for the railway and no work for the terminals. Would it not be the part of wisdom to suspend work on the terminals and go ahead at reasonable speed with the building of the railway; and would it not be reasonable, instead of taking the material by steamer to Port Nelson, to construct the line first, and so bring in material for the harbour works by rail, and in the meantime operating the line by giving a reasonable service sufficient to carry the traffic, that can be developed? Instead of that, in order to build this road and these terminals, you propose to tax every one who mails a letter. The poor woman who mails a letter, it may be to her son fighting in the trenches, is asked to contribute this extra alleged war stamp. And why? To build the Hudson Bay railway and create the terminals there. I contend that no work should be carried on during the present year unless it is of an urgent character, one the failure to prosecute which would cause the interests of the country inevitably to suffer.
Then, take the Quebec harbour. We are asked for $1,200,000 for a dry-dock there.

Well, they have a very fair dry-dock at Quebec. I recognize the importance of building a dry-dock there, but is it necessary to spend the whole $1,200,000? If $600,000 were expended there during the coming year it would do	a
great deal of work and would give employment to a large number of people. Then there is $450,000 for the French river waterway improvement for which last year $500,000 was voted and only $50,000 of which was expended. That being so, could not you reasonably postpone the expenditure of at least a part of this $450,000 until the war is over and the condition of the people improved?

The time to spend
money is when times are hard, so as to provide work for the people.

That is right, if you
have the money in the treasury. But is this the time to tax the people of this country, when, as I have said every dollar, every cent they can spare is being given to charity? The same remarks would apply to other harbours-Toronto, where you propose to spend $1,000,000; Vancouver, $1,000,000; Victoria, $1,400,000. Take these items on page 57 of the Estimates, to some of which I have referred, and you will find that where the minister last year asked for $12,780,000, ho did not expend within $3,159,200 of it. Yet the amount is being carried forward as a re-vote and forms part of what is to be voted this year.
The total vote is $9,000,000 less.
The total vote for railways, canals and public works, including the harbours and public buildings, is $1,000,000 more than the amount expended last year.

I was referring to the
amounts on page 57.
On those items the minister asks the same amount as he expended last year.
Last year the minister asked, for these items on page 57 which are chargeable to capital, $12,780,500, and this year he is asking for $9,459,200, or more than $3,000,000 less-
Less than what?
Less than he asked for last year.
But what did he expend?

He spent $9,000,000. But
that does not say that he will spend that amount this year.
That is exactly the argument.

And the amount asked
for this year is $3,000,000 less than it was last year. So, the amount for both departments is many millions less than last year.

Exactly what I said; I thank the hon. minister for corroborating my statement. I said these departments spent last year $18,000,000 less than they asked for under the Main Estimates and Supplementary Estimates combined. Today the two ministers are asking for $1,000,000 more than they actually expended last year. My argument is that with prudence, with the exercise of a little judgment, they could get along with $18,000,000 or $20,000,000 less than they are asking for in the Estimates. Now, take Harbours and Rivers, chargeable to income. I cannot speak of other places, but I will speak of my own constituency. The hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) knows that he has an amount- $100,000, I think-to extend the breakwater to Partridge Island. But he has announced publicly that he is not going to commence that work this year. Why, then, is it in the Estimates, except for the reason I suggested-that the minister thinks it proper to keep it there because it will be easier to get it voted when he wishes to go ahead. But why raise a war tax-
I do not remember having made the public statement that I do not intend to go on with the breakwater to Partridge Island.
Let me ask, then, if the hon. minister intends to go on with it?
We have called for tenders, and I am hopeful that we shall be able to go on, because that is one of the most important works in the Dominion I believe.
The statement has been .made publicly that the new works will not be gone on with during the present year.
That is not a new work.

Entirely new. The
present breakwater has been completed for thirty years.
It is part of the harbour.

Yes, but still it is a
new work. Then again the Department of Railways asks for $112,000 to build the spur line to Courtenay Bay.
Parliament granted that money at least three years ago, and not a blow has been struck, although we voted and revoted the money, and it is put in again this year. I venture to say that there is no intention of going ahead with that work this year. I am sorry that by reason of the bungling and humbugging and the mistakes that have been made in connection with the Valley railway and the carrying of the Transcontinental to the port of St. John, it is not very likely that anything will be done on that spur line during the present year. The Provincial Government and the Minister of Railways do not know how they are going to bring the Valley railway into the harbour of St. John. They have reached Gagetown, they commenced at Centreville in Carleton county-the road begins nowhere and ends nowhere. The only thing which they have is an agreement-which, fortunately, I was able to negotiate with my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals-that the Dominion Government shoulcj undertake operation as each 40 miles were completed. But our scheme was to build from the city of St. John to Grand Falls, there to connect with the Transcontinental railway so that the Valley line might be utilized as part of the Transcontinental system. I say the matter has been humbugged and trifled with, mistakes have been made, grades have been altered between Fredericton and the country to the north, and there does not seem to be any reasonable probability that the line can be used with success as a part of the Transcontinental system. While the Provincial Government and this Government do not say publicly that the road is not to go to St. John, I am told that the Minister of Railways is pretty sure that it is not going to St. John, and that he is going to carry it over to Westfield to connect with the Canadian Pacific railway. It may be that that is the reason why this spur line to Courtenay bay has not been built. At all events, if it is not to be built this year, I decidedly object to the people being taxed to build it-the tax being called a war tax-when it is not proposed to go ahead with it at all during the coming year. The same applies to hundreds of other items in these Estimates.
With regard to public buildings. In the item for Ontario there are 106 or more public buildings, and in respect of nearly every one there is a revote. The total vote for Ontario
is $3,905,100. The amount voted last year in both main and supplementary Estimates was $4,771,200.56; yet there is a revote of the enormous sum of $2,282,100. In other words, practically 50 per cent of the amount which my hon. friend had placed in the Estimates for public buildings in Ontario last year has not been expended, and is being carried forward as a re-vote. Did my hon. friend seriously intend to go ahead with those public buildings at that time, or did he, upon the persistent request of his friends from Ontario, put them there in order to obviate the danger of any question arising as to whether public buildings were or were not to be erected? The blue book is always authoritative; it counts for so much more than the mere statement of the member. While $3,354,750 was voted last year for public buildings in Quebec, in respect of nearly every one of them a very large amount is carried over as a re-vote, showing that no contracts have been entered into, that no work has been done; and that in respect of many of these buildings-there is no urgency except political urgency.
There is no political urgency at all. There may have been urgency in my hon. friend's day, but there is none in mine.
I am sure that my hon. friend is not altogether unaware of the fact that constituencies are to a certain extent influenced by the consideration as to whether or not they are to get public buildings.
Not those represented on this side of the House.

Of course, it may be
that my hon. friend would prefer to exercise other influences than the mere production of the blue book to the electors. I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at 10.07 p.m.
Friday, February 26, 1915.
